summary.text: Writing an odd integer as \(2n+1\), the assumed representation gives the required Lemoine decomposition when \(n>30\), while the cases \(3\le n\le30\) are handled by explicit prime decompositions. If there were only finitely many twin primes, the admissible primes \(p\) would form a finite nonempty set because \(p\mapsto \operatorname{prime}(p+2)\) injects it into the twin primes; taking their odd product \(P\) and applying the hypothesis to \(21P=2n+1=2p+q\) forces \(p\mid q\) with \(1<p<q\), contradicting the primality of \(q\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(r_j\) denote the \(j\)-th prime in the usual one-indexed ordering, so
\[
r_1=2,\quad r_2=3,\quad r_3=5,\quad r_4=7,\ldots.
\]
Thus the expression \(\operatorname{prime}(p+2)\) in the conjecture is \(r_{p+2}\).

Assume part (ii) of the conjecture: for every natural number \(n>30\), there are primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
r_{p+2}+2
\]
is prime and
\[
2n+1=2p+q. \tag{1}
\]
We prove separately that this assumption implies Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.

## 1. Lemoine’s conjecture

Let \(k>5\) be odd. Since \(k\) is odd, it has the form
\[
k=2n+1
\]
for some natural number \(n\). The inequality \(k>5\) implies \(n\ge 3\).

First suppose \(n>30\). Apply part (ii) to this \(n\). We obtain primes \(p,q\) satisfying (1). Reordering the two summands gives
\[
k=2n+1=q+2p.
\]
Thus \(k\) is a prime plus twice a prime, as required by Lemoine’s conjecture. Notice that the additional condition that \(r_{p+2}+2\) is prime is not needed for this part of the argument.

It remains to treat \(3\le n\le 30\), equivalently the odd integers \(7\le k\le 61\). The following table explicitly writes each such \(k=2n+1\) in the form \(a+2b\), with both \(a\) and \(b\) prime:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n&k=2n+1&k=a+2b\\ \hline
3&7&3+2\cdot2\\
4&9&5+2\cdot2\\
5&11&7+2\cdot2\\
6&13&3+2\cdot5\\
7&15&11+2\cdot2\\
8&17&13+2\cdot2\\
9&19&5+2\cdot7\\
10&21&17+2\cdot2\\
11&23&19+2\cdot2\\
12&25&19+2\cdot3\\
13&27&23+2\cdot2\\
14&29&23+2\cdot3\\
15&31&17+2\cdot7\\
16&33&29+2\cdot2\\
17&35&29+2\cdot3\\
18&37&31+2\cdot3\\
19&39&29+2\cdot5\\
20&41&37+2\cdot2\\
21&43&37+2\cdot3\\
22&45&41+2\cdot2\\
23&47&43+2\cdot2\\
24&49&43+2\cdot3\\
25&51&47+2\cdot2\\
26&53&47+2\cdot3\\
27&55&41+2\cdot7\\
28&57&53+2\cdot2\\
29&59&53+2\cdot3\\
30&61&47+2\cdot7
\end{array}
\]
All numbers used as \(a\) or \(b\) in this table are primes. This covers every remaining odd \(k>5\). Hence every odd integer greater than \(5\) is a prime plus twice a prime, proving Lemoine’s conjecture.

## 2. The twin prime conjecture

We now prove that there are infinitely many primes \(s\) for which \(s+2\) is also prime.

Suppose, for contradiction, that the set of twin-prime lower members
\[
\mathcal U=\{s\in\mathbb N: s\text{ and }s+2\text{ are prime}\}
\]
is finite.

Define the set of admissible parameters
\[
T=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }r_{p+2}+2\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
For every \(p\in T\), the number \(r_{p+2}\) is prime by definition of the prime sequence, and \(r_{p+2}+2\) is prime by the defining condition of \(T\). Therefore
\[
p\longmapsto r_{p+2}
\]
maps \(T\) into \(\mathcal U\).

This map is injective: the sequence of primes \(r_1,r_2,r_3,\ldots\) is strictly increasing, so \(r_{a+2}=r_{b+2}\) implies \(a+2=b+2\), and hence \(a=b\). Since \(T\) injects into the finite set \(\mathcal U\), the set \(T\) is finite.

We record two further facts about \(T\). First,
\[
2\notin T.
\]
Indeed, \(r_{2+2}=r_4=7\), and \(r_4+2=9\) is not prime. Consequently every member of \(T\), being a prime other than \(2\), is odd and at least \(3\).

Second, \(T\) is nonempty. Apply part (ii) with \(n=31\). It supplies primes \(p_0,q_0\) such that \(r_{p_0+2}+2\) is prime and
\[
63=2p_0+q_0.
\]
The first and third of these properties say exactly that \(p_0\in T\).

Because \(T\) is finite and nonempty, form the positive integer
\[
P=\prod_{t\in T}t.
\]
Every factor is a positive odd prime, so \(P\) is positive and odd. Moreover, \(p_0\mid P\); since \(P>0\), this implies \(p_0\le P\). As \(p_0\ge3\), we have
\[
P\ge3. \tag{2}
\]

Now consider
\[
M=21P.
\]
Both \(21\) and \(P\) are odd, so \(M\) is odd. Hence there is a natural number \(n\) such that
\[
21P=2n+1. \tag{3}
\]
By (2), \(21P\ge63\). Equation (3) therefore gives \(2n+1\ge63\), so \(n\ge31\), in particular \(n>30\).

Apply part (ii) to this \(n\). We obtain primes \(p,q\), with \(r_{p+2}+2\) prime, such that
\[
2n+1=2p+q.
\]
Together with (3), this is
\[
21P=2p+q. \tag{4}
\]
Since \(p\) is prime and \(r_{p+2}+2\) is prime, we have \(p\in T\). By the definition of \(P\), every member of \(T\) divides \(P\), and therefore
\[
p\mid P.
\]
In particular \(p\le P\), because \(P>0\), and also \(p\mid21P\). Of course \(p\mid2p\). Subtracting the term \(2p\) in (4), or equivalently reducing (4) modulo \(p\), yields
\[
p\mid q. \tag{5}
\]

On the other hand, (4) and \(p\le P\) show that
\[
q=21P-2p\ge21P-2P=19P.
\]
Since \(P>0\), we have \(19P>P\ge p\), and hence
\[
q>p. \tag{6}
\]

But \(q\) is prime. Every positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. By (5), \(p\) is a divisor of \(q\). Since \(p\) is itself prime, \(p\ne1\), so necessarily \(p=q\). This contradicts (6).

The contradiction shows that \(\mathcal U\) cannot be finite. Thus infinitely many primes \(s\) have \(s+2\) prime, which is the twin prime conjecture.

We have proved that part (ii) of the A236566 conjecture implies both Lemoine’s conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.
